title: 3SUM: all triples vs sorting with two pointers
problem_statement: Given n integers a_1..a_n, decide whether there are indices i < j < k with a_i + a_j + a_k = 0.

input.size_measure: n machine words (values bounded by O(n^2) in the harness).

algorithms.name: all triples
algorithms.pseudocode: for i < j < k: if a_i + a_j + a_k = 0: yes

algorithms.name: sort + two pointers
algorithms.idea: Sort. For each i, move pointers j (from the left) and k (from the right) over a[i+1..n-1] toward each other, depending on the sign of the sum.
algorithms.correctness: For fixed i the pair sums a[j] + a[k] are monotone in j and k on the sorted array, so the two-pointer scan never skips a solution.

lower_bounds.bound: no O(n^(2-eps)) algorithm for any eps > 0
lower_bounds.setting: conjectured (the 3SUM conjecture, basis of 3SUM-hardness; Gajentaan & Overmars 1995)

relationship: Theta(n^3) -> Theta(n^2). The 3SUM conjecture states that no O(n^(2-eps)) algorithm exists for any eps > 0. Grønlund & Pettie 2014 gave o(n^2) by log factors, and linear decision trees need only O(n log^2 n) comparisons (Kane, Lovett & Moran 2019), so the conjecture is about algorithms, not decision-tree depth.

sources.title: On a class of O(n^2) problems in computational geometry

sources.authors: Kane, D. M.; Lovett, S.; Moran, S.
sources.title: Near-optimal Linear Decision Trees for k-SUM and Related Problems

verification.method: V1: both agree with each other and with an independent hash-based oracle on random instances with values in [-n^2, n^2] (yes and no answers both occur), n = 0..60 for the cubic algorithm. V2: worst-case instances (no solution, so no early exit) fitted against n^3 and n^2.

caveats: The 3SUM conjecture is a hypothesis, not a theorem; many geometric problems are '3SUM-hard' relative to it.
notes: A hub of fine-grained complexity, alongside SETH (edit distance, LCS) and APSP.
